Can microaeration and hydraulic retention time steer anaerobic 
microbiomes toward efficient linear alkylbenzene sulfonate degradation?
Maurício Guimar˜aes de Oliveira
, Vicente Elício Porfiro Sales Gonçalves da Silva,  
Steven Renato Ferreira Vasconcelos, Paulo Igor Milen Firmino, Andr´e Bezerra dos Santos *
Department of Hydraulic and Environmental Engineering, Federal University of Cear´a, Fortaleza, Cear´a, Brazil
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• Microaeration combined with 16-h HRT 
increases LAS removal to 64%.
• The 16-h HRT prevents washout of 
specialized microaerophilic consortia.
• Specific methane yield reached 0.28 
LCH4/gCODapp, doubling the anaerobic 
control.
• High Thauera and Desulfovibrio abun­
dances are associated with enhanced 
LAS removal.
• Synergy between redox zones over­
comes the kinetic barriers of surfactant 
toxicity.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic-microaerophilic consortium
Surfactant biodegradation
Specific methane yield
Aromatic ring cleavage
Metabolicoxygenases
Waste-to-energy efficiency
A B S T R A C T
The sustainable treatment of surfactant-rich wastewater in anaerobic systems is often hindered by the 
biochemical recalcitrance of linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS) and its inhibitory effects on methanogenesis. 
This study investigated controlled microaeration under two hydraulic retention time (HRT) and organic loading 
rate (OLR) regimes as a strategy to intensify LAS degradation and energy recovery in upflow anaerobic sludge 
blanket (UASB) reactors. Four configurations were evaluated: R1 (anaerobic, 8-h HRT), R2 (microaerated, 8-h 
HRT), R3 (anaerobic, 16-h HRT), and R4 (microaerated, 16-h HRT). Results demonstrated that under strictly 
anaerobic conditions, operating at a 16-h HRT and the corresponding lower OLR resulted in higher chemical 
oxygen demand (COD) removal than at 8-h HRT (87.4% vs. 65.7%). In contrast, microaeration played an 
important role in enhancing surfactant biotransformation. R4 achieved the highest LAS removal (64.0 ± 6.2%), 
significantly outperforming the strictly anaerobic R3. The 16-h HRT/lower-OLR configuration provided opera­
tional conditions that may have favored the progression of successive LAS biotransformation steps, including 
oxygenase-mediated ω-oxidation and the transformation of aromatic compounds under microaerated conditions. 
Notably, R4 exhibited a remarkable specific methane yield of 0.28 ± 0.01 LCH4/gCODapp, doubling the efficiency 
of the other reactors. Microbial analysis indicated that microaeration was associated with a more diverse con­
sortium in which potentially oxidative bacteria (Smithella and Thauera) coexisted with acetoclastic methanogens 
(Methanosaeta). These findings indicate that microaeration, when combined with the longer HRT tested,

1. Introduction
Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS) is a widely used anionic sur­
factant that is frequently detected in domestic wastewater at concen­
trations of 0.8–21 mg⋅L⁻1 (Costa et al., 2024; Motteran et al., 2018). Its 
incomplete removal in conventional treatment plants results in envi­
ronmental accumulation and adverse effects, including foam formation 
and impaired oxygen transfer, while its surfactant properties may also 
disrupt microbial membranes and inhibit biological activity at elevated 
concentrations (Luo et al., 2023; Teran et al., 2022). In upflow anaerobic 
sludge blanket (UASB) reactors, LAS removal typically ranges from 30% 
to 91%, a process that is highly dependent on the availability of 
fermentable co-substrates, such as ethanol or sucrose, to sustain syn­
trophic pathways and mitigate surfactant-induced metabolic stress 
(Costa et al., 2024; Terreros-Mecalco et al., 2024).
Despite these reported efficiencies, anaerobic LAS biodegradation 
remains challenging because its amphiphilic structure combines a hy­
drophobic alkyl chain with a sulfonated aromatic moiety. Interactions of 
the hydrophobic moiety with sludge and cell membranes can restrict 
bioavailability and inhibit microbial activity, whereas degradation of 
the aromatic structure requires initial activation. Under strictly anaer­
obic conditions, this activation may occur via fumarate addition, fol­
lowed by β-oxidation, desulfonation, and aromatic ring transformation 
(Cui et al., 2022; Lara-Martín et al., 2010). These kinetically constrained 
reactions, together with surfactant-induced microbial inhibition, 
constitute major bottlenecks for LAS biodegradation, particularly at 
short contact times (Terreros-Mecalco et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2020).
Hydraulic retention time (HRT) is therefore an important opera­
tional parameter, as it determines the contact time available for these 
complex biotransformation steps. Granatto et al. (2019) achieved 60 ±
30% LAS removal in an Expanded Granular Sludge Bed (EGSB) reactor 
at an HRT of 36 h. In contrast, Carosia et al. (2014) reported 48 ± 10% 
in an Anaerobic Fluidized Bed Reactor (AFBR) at 15 h. In UASB reactors, 
Okada et al. (2013) reported only 18% LAS removal at an HRT of 6 h. 
However, extending the HRT requires larger reactor volumes and may 
compromise the economic advantages of UASB technology, particularly 
for domestic wastewater treatment, where HRTs of 6–8 h are commonly 
used (Chernicharo et al., 2015). Thus, strategies that alleviate kinetic 
limitations without relying exclusively on prolonged residence times are 
particularly relevant for LAS treatment.
Microaeration represents a potential strategy because controlled 
oxygen supplementation can promote initial oxidative transformations 
of recalcitrant compounds while preserving predominantly anaerobic 
conditions and the associated potential for energy recovery. Reported 
oxygen doses range from 0.005 to 5 L O2⋅Lfeed
-1 ⋅d-1 depending on the 
treatment objective and substrate composition (de Oliveira et al., 2021; 
Nguyen and Khanal, 2018).
Previous studies have demonstrated that controlled oxygen supple­
mentation can substantially enhance the biotransformation of recalci­
trant compounds in predominantly anaerobic systems. For BTEX, 
Siqueira et al. (2018) reported removal efficiencies ranging from 55 to 
82% under strictly anaerobic conditions, whereas microaeration at 
0.5–2.0 mLair⋅min⁻1 increased removal to above 83% for all compounds 
under the best-performing conditions. At an airflow rate of 1.0 
mLair⋅min⁻1, benzene removal increased from 54.9 to 83.9% and toluene 
removal from 67.3 to 88.6%, while ethylbenzene and xylenes also 
achieved removals above 85%. Notably, increasing the airflow rate to 
2.0 mLair⋅min⁻1 did not further improve BTEX removal, highlighting the 
importance of controlled rather than excessive oxygen supplementation. 
Similar benefits of microaeration have been reported for other recalci­
trant organic compounds (do Nascimento et al., 2021; Carvalho et al., 
2020), supporting its potential as a process-intensification strategy that 
facilitates otherwise kinetically constrained biotransformation steps 
while preserving the advantages of predominantly anaerobic treatment.
More recently, Ortiz-Ardila et al. (2024) demonstrated that microa­
eration enhanced the conversion of volatile D4 and D5 siloxanes to 
methane and simpler products, while reshaping the anaerobic microbial 
community. Despite the structural differences between siloxanes and 
LAS, these findings reinforce the broader concept that controlled oxygen 
supplementation can facilitate initial transformation steps of recalci­
trant compounds while preserving downstream anaerobic processes, 
including methanogenesis.
From this structural perspective, microaeration offers a feasible 
means to alleviate one of the main bottlenecks in anaerobic LAS 
degradation by supplying limited amounts of molecular oxygen to 
initiate molecular activation while preserving predominantly anaerobic 
conditions. Oxygen can support mono- and dioxygenase-mediated re­
actions involved in terminal hydroxylation of the alkyl chain (ω-oxida­
tion) and subsequent transformations of the aromatic moiety, 
generating more hydrophilic carboxylated intermediates that are more 
accessible to downstream biodegradation (Cui et al., 2022; Liu et al., 
2024). Thus, rather than replacing anaerobic metabolism, microaeration 
may act as an oxidative priming step that facilitates the transformation 
of structurally recalcitrant LAS into intermediates more amenable to 
subsequent anaerobic metabolic reactions (Lara-Martín et al., 2010; Xu 
et al., 2023).
Beyond enzymatic activation, microaeration combined with 
fermentable co-substrates, such as sucrose, may promote functional se­
lection within the microbial community. This process favors the 
enrichment of a specialized microaerophilic-syntrophic consortium, 
notably dominated by the phylum Pseudomonadota and genera such as 
Pleomorphomonas and Desulfovibrio (Buarque et al., 2019; do Nascimento 
et al., 2021). This specialized structure facilitates a coupled metabolic 
sequence: an initial oxidative attack on the LAS molecule, followed by 
anaerobic desulfonation and methanogenesis by oxygen-tolerant 
archaea such as Methanobacterium. Consequently, microaeration 
bridges the efficiency of aerobic pathways with the energy recovery of 
anaerobic digestion without compromising process stability (Costa 
et al., 2024).
Despite the documented benefits of microaeration in anaerobic sys­
tems, its effect on LAS treatment under different hydraulic and organic 
loading conditions remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study 
evaluated microaeration under two operationally distinct HRT/OLR 
regimes. Therefore, this study compared two operationally distinct 
HRTs, 8 and 16 h, under anaerobic and microaerated conditions. The 8-h 
HRT is a short residence time commonly used in high-rate UASB sys­
tems. In contrast, the 16-h HRT served as a longer-residence-time 
benchmark to assess whether extending substrate–biomass contact 
could alleviate kinetic limitations.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental set-up
Four lab-scale UASB reactors (working volume of 3.5 L) (Fig. 1), 
inoculated with anaerobic sludge [Total solids (TS) = 55.1 ± 3.5 g⋅L−1, 
total volatile solids (TVS) = 30.6 ± 1.4 = g⋅L−1 and total fixed solids 
(TFS) = 24.7 ± 1.1 g⋅L−1], were operated, in parallel, at a room tem­
perature of approximately 28 ◦C.
The reactors were operated under the same conditions except for 
microaeration and HRT. R1 and R3 were conventional UASB reactors, 
while R2 and R4 included microaeration and were referred to as UMSB

(Upflow Microaerobic Sludge Blanket). Regarding hydraulic retention 
time, R1 and R2 had an HRT of 8 h, while R3 and R4 had an HRT of 16 h. 
The 16-h HRT was selected as a strategic benchmark to confirm that any 
performance limitations at 8 h were kinetic rather than due to inoculum 
or system instability. This approach is based on prior research by the 
group, which showed that short residence times led to only 32 ± 16% 
LAS removal in the microaerobic system (de Oliveira et al., 2026).
Microaeration was performed with synthetic air (80% N2:20% O2, 
White Martins, Brazil) from the bottom of the reactor, using a mass flow 
controller (GFC17, Cole-Parmer, USA). The microaeration air dose used 
in R2 and R4 was approximately 1.5 mLair⋅min−1, corresponding to 
0.041 e 0.082 L O2⋅Lfeed
-1 ⋅d-1, respectively. The gas was introduced at the 
bottom of each reactor through a bubble diffuser, promoting its 
dispersion into the liquid phase along the upflow path. The microaera­
tion dose was selected based on the best results reported by do 
Nascimento et al. (2021)
for the removal of emerging sulfur- 
containing compounds.
The reactors were fed with synthetic wastewater containing the LAS 
(Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate, 100%, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) (15 
mg⋅L−1), sucrose (1 g COD⋅L−1), basal medium (macro and micro­
nutrients) prepared according to Firmino et al. (2010), and sodium bi­
carbonate (1 g⋅L−1) to maintain the pH close to 7.0. The organic loading 
rates (OLRs) were 3.0 g COD⋅L⁻1⋅d⁻1 for R1 and R2 (8-h HRT) and 1.5 g 
COD⋅L⁻1⋅d⁻1 for R3 and R4 (16-h HRT). All reagents were used as pur­
chased without further purification. The synthetic influent was kept 
refrigerated at 4 ◦C to prevent natural biodegradation of organic matter.
2.2. Chemical and chromatographic analysis
Chemical oxygen demand (COD), pH, TSS, and TS content were 
determined according to APHA (2012).
The quantification of CH4, CO2, H2, and H2S in the biogas was 
determined by gas chromatography with ionization detection by 
dielectric barrier discharge (GC BID-2010 Plus, Shimadzu Corporation, 
Japan), equipped with a GS-GASPRO column (60 m × 0.32 mm) (Agilent 
Technologies Inc., USA). Helium gas (White Martins LTDA, Brazil) was 
used as the carrier gas at a flow rate of 2 mL⋅min−1, with a run time of 9 
min. Oven, injector, and detector temperatures were 50, 100, and 
250 ◦C, respectively. O2 and N2 were quantified by gas chromatography 
with thermal conductivity detection (GC-TCD) (GC-17A, Shimadzu 
Corporation, Japan). The biogas sample (1.0 mL) was injected in split­
less mode, and chromatographic separation was performed on a Mol 
Sieve 5A PLOT column (30 m, 0.32 mm ID) (Restek Corporation, USA). 
Oven, injector, and detector temperatures were 35, 40, and 230 ◦C, 
respectively. Helium (White Martins, Brazil) was used as the carrier gas 
at a flow rate of 7 mL⋅min−1, and the run time was 5 min.
LAS concentrations were determined by high-performance liquid 
chromatography (HPLC) using a Shimadzu system (CBM-20A, SPD-20A, 
CTO-20A, SIL-20A, and LC-20AT) equipped with a reversed-phase C18 
column from Shimadzu, as described by Silva et al. (2017). The mobile 
phase was water with 5 mmol⋅L−1 ammonium acetate (solvent A) and 
acetonitrile (solvent B); the mobile phase flow rate was 1 mL⋅min−1, the 
sample volume was 50 µL, the temperature of the thermostated 
compartment of the column was 40 ◦C, and UV–Vis detection at 230 nm. 
A gradient was applied to the mobile phase to separate the LAS con­
stituents; it started at 45% solvent B, which began to rise after 5 min and 
reached 60% in 20 min, then returned to 45% after 1 min and remained 
at 45% for 6 min. Volumetric LAS removal rates were calculated from 
the difference between influent and effluent LAS concentrations, 
considering the influent flow rate and the working volume of each 
reactor, and were expressed as mg LAS⋅Lreactor
-1
⋅d-1.
2.3. Off-gas oxygen depletion analysis
To provide an independent assessment of oxygen depletion under 
microaeration, the O2 and N2 concentrations in the reactor off-gas were 
monitored throughout the operational period and used to calculate the 
off-gas O2/N2 ratio. Nitrogen was used as an internal tracer because it is 
expected to behave conservatively under the evaluated operational 
conditions, whereas oxygen may be transferred to the liquid phase and 
depleted through oxidative processes.

2.4. Statistical analysis
The Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric tests, which 
do not require specific distributional assumptions, were used to compare 
reactor performance across the different experimental periods at the 5% 
significance level.
2.5. Microbiological analysis
Composite sludge samples were collected from all reactors at the 
beginning and end of each operational period. Total DNA was extracted 
from 0.25 g of fresh biomass using the PowerSoil® DNA Isolation Kit 
(MoBio Laboratories Inc., USA). The V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was 
amplified in triplicate using specific primers 515F/806R. Post- 
amplification, products were purified with Agencourt AMPure XP 
beads (Beckman Coulter) and quantified using the Qubit 2.0 fluorimeter 
(Invitrogen). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq platform 
using 300-cycle chemistry.
Bioinformatics processing was conducted using the DADA2 package 
v1.28.0 to filter and assemble reads into amplicon sequencing variants 
(ASVs) (Callahan et al., 2016). Taxonomic classification was assigned 
using the MiDAS database v5.1, which is specialized for anaerobic 
digestion consortia.
Alpha diversity indices were calculated using the Phyloseq package 
v1.44.0. Metabolic functional profiles were predicted from the 16S 
rRNA gene sequencing data using PICRUSt2 (Phylogenetic Investigation 
of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States 2), and pre­
dicted gene families were annotated based on KEGG Orthologs (KOs). 
The resulting predictions were used to compare the potential represen­
tation of metabolic functions among the microbial communities of the 
different reactors.
Raw sequence data are available in the NCBI BioProject database 
under ID PRJNA836880.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of the UASB reactors
3.1.1. Operational parameters and volumetric biogas production
The monitoring of pH and Acidity/TA ratios showed no statistically 
significant differences between the reactors (p > 0.05), indicating that 
the system maintained a stable buffering capacity regardless of the HRT 
or the redox environment (Fig. S1). All reactors operated within an 
alkaline pH range (7.6–8.0), which is optimal for methanogenic activity.
The Acidity/TA ratios remained consistently above the 0.3 threshold 
(0.5–0.6) across all treatments. This absence of statistical variance 
suggests that the accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) was a 
common characteristic of the influent (sucrose + LAS) rather than a 
result of operational changes. The stability of these parameters dem­
onstrates that neither the high organic load at 8-h HRT nor the oxygen 
supply in the microaerated systems (R2 and R4) compromised the global 
metabolic balance, thereby enabling subsequent evaluation of LAS 
removal under a stabilized anaerobic-microaerophilic environment.
The biogas dynamics reflected the combined influence of the oper­
ational conditions and redox environment (Fig. 2). Among the strictly 
anaerobic reactors, R1, operated at an 8-h HRT and the corresponding 
higher OLR, showed a higher volumetric methane production (1.2 ± 0.1 
LCH4⋅d⁻1) than R3 (1.0 ± 0.1 LCH4⋅d⁻1), operated at a 16-h HRT and lower 
OLR (p = 0.043). Because the influent COD concentration was main­
tained constant, decreasing the HRT from 16 to 8 h by increasing the 
influent flow rate concomitantly increased the OLR from approximately 
1.5 to 3.0 g COD⋅L⁻1⋅d⁻1. Therefore, the difference in volumetric 
methane production between R1 and R3 cannot be attributed solely to 
either HRT or OLR; rather, it reflects the combined effect of these 
coupled operational parameters.
In the microaerated reactors, R2 and R4 exhibited total gas flow rates 
of 9.6 and 4.7 L⋅d⁻1, respectively. These values include the externally 
supplied synthetic air and therefore cannot be interpreted exclusively as 
biologically produced biogas. Nevertheless, absolute methane produc­
tion can be directly compared between the reactors and was approxi­
mately twofold higher in R2 than in R4 (2.6 vs. 1.4 LCH4⋅d⁻1, p < 0.001). 
This difference is consistent with their hydraulic operation: because R2 
was operated at half the HRT of R4 (8 vs. 16 h) at the same influent COD 
concentration, its daily influent flow and, consequently, COD load were 
approximately twice those of R4. Thus, the greater absolute methane 
production in R2 primarily reflects the greater amount of organic sub­
strate supplied per unit time rather than evidence of a higher methane 
conversion efficiency.
Methane content also differed between the microaerated reactors. R4 
(16 h) achieved 30 ± 2% CH4, nearly reaching the 45% energy recovery 
threshold (de Oliveira et al., 2026), whereas R2 (8 h) exhibited a lower 
CH4 content of 26 ± 2%. Since both reactors received the same airflow 
rate, the higher CH4 fraction in R4 indicates a more favorable balance 
between methane generation and the total gas flow under this opera­
tional condition. This gas quality is comparable to that observed by 
Buarque et al. (2019) under the same operating conditions.
More importantly, comparison within each HRT showed greater 
absolute methane production under microaeration. At 8 h, methane 
production increased from 1.2 ± 0.1 L⋅d⁻1 in R1 to approximately 2.6 
LCH4⋅d⁻1 in R2 (p < 0.001), whereas at 16 h it increased from 1.0 ± 0.1 
LCH4⋅d⁻1 in R3 to approximately 1.4 LCH4⋅d⁻1 in R4 (p = 0,022). Because 
each anaerobic–microaerated pair was operated at the same HRT and 
corresponding OLR, these comparisons provide a more direct indication 
of the association between microaeration and methane production than 
comparisons across different HRTs. These results surpass the yields re­
ported by Okada et al. (2013), who found that anaerobic reactors 
treating high LAS concentrations (up to 40 mg⋅L⁻1) exhibited significant 
methanogenic inhibition and lower volumetric production. The higher 
methane production observed under microaeration is consistent with 
the possibility that limited oxygen supplementation alleviated some of 
the constraints imposed by LAS on methanogenic activity, as also sug­
gested for micro-oxygenated systems treating sulfonated aromatic 
compounds (Zhou et al., 2022).
3.1.2. Efficiency parameters
COD removal efficiency across all experimental systems ranged from 
65.7 ± 12.3% to 87.4 ± 3.4%, with the 16-h/lower-OLR configuration 
generally showing higher organic matter removal. In both strictly 
anaerobic and microaerated regimes, doubling the residence time from 
8 h (R1 and R2) to 16 h (R3 and R4) resulted in the highest and most 
consistent removal rates (Fig. 3). This trend indicates that the 8-h HRT 
imposes kinetic limitations on the consortia, likely exacerbated by LAS 
inhibition, which hinders the full stabilization of the sucrose-based 
influent regardless of the aeration status.
Microaeration served as an effective oxidative boost, particularly at 
the shorter HRT. R2 (8 h, microaerated) achieved 77.6 ± 6.8%, signif­
icantly outperforming its anaerobic counterpart (R1) (p = 0.042). This 
improvement can be attributed to the stimulation of facultative

Normalization of methane production by the applied COD load 
provided a different perspective than the volumetric production results,

and the 8-h microaerated reactor (R2) showed average yields of 0.11 ±

This performance significantly exceeds the yields reported by Duarte 
et al. (2010), who observed specific methane yields around 0.2 LCH4/ 
gCODapp in UASB reactors treating LAS under strictly anaerobic condi­
tions, where surfactant toxicity limited methanogenic efficiency. The

demonstrates that controlled oxygenation acts as a process intensifier. 
This trend is supported by Delforno et al. (2012), who reported that 
introducing oxygen-mediated stages into the treatment of anionic sur­
factants led to more robust aromatic ring degradation, thereby 
increasing the availability of acetate for methanogens and boosting 
specific methane production relative to purely anaerobic benchmarks. 
By overcoming the typical kinetic barriers of surfactant-rich wastewater, 
R4 maximized the conversion of the applied organic load into energy.
Although R2 exhibited almost twice the absolute methane produc­
tion of R4 (2.6 vs. 1.4 LCH4⋅d⁻1), normalization by the applied COD load 
reversed this relationship, with R4 showing a higher specific methane 
yield than R2. This distinction indicates that the greater volumetric 
methane production at the 8-h HRT was largely associated with its 
higher daily organic load. In contrast, the 16-h microaerated condition 
converted a greater fraction of the applied COD into methane.
The higher specific methane yield observed under microaeration 
suggests that limited oxygen supplementation did not compromise 
methanogenesis and may have favored the conversion of the applied 
organic load into methane. A plausible explanation is that microaeration 
facilitated initial transformations of recalcitrant organic compounds, 
potentially increasing the availability of intermediates for subsequent 
anaerobic metabolism (Chen et al., 2020). However, because interme­
diate products and metabolic fluxes were not directly characterized, the 
mechanisms underlying the enhanced methane yield cannot be 
conclusively established from the present data.
3.2. Removal of linear alkylbenzene sulfonate
LAS removal varied with operational conditions, with efficiencies 
ranging from 34.8% (R1) to 64.0% (R4) (Fig. 4). During the early 
operational phase, all four reactors achieved average LAS removal effi­
ciencies exceeding 70%, with no statistically significant differences be­
tween the systems (p = 0.65). This performance is linked to the high 
functional diversity of the incipient anaerobic microbiota, which had 
not yet been subjected to the selective pressure of sulfonated com­
pounds. At this stage, the likely minimal accumulation of toxic in­
termediates, combined with the absence of chronic stress, favored the 
activity of consortia capable of at least partially degrading xenobiotics. 
Furthermore, because LAS concentrations remained below inhibitory 
thresholds, microbial activity was not significantly suppressed, allowing 
broad, nonspecific metabolic pathways to participate in the initial co- 
metabolic transformation.
The chemical nature of the pollutant dictates the shift from initial 
transformation to long-term stability. Specifically, the highly stable 
sulfonated aromatic ring and the hydrophobic alkyl chain of LAS impose 
severe thermodynamic constraints under strictly anaerobic conditions 
(R1 and R3). In the absence of molecular oxygen, benzene ring cleavage 
is restricted to the multi-step benzoyl-CoA pathway. This slow reductive 
route is frequently hindered by the molecule's inherent toxicity (Fu 
et al., 2023), thus limiting the overall rate of organic matter 
stabilization.
In strictly anaerobic systems, doubling the HRT from 8 h (R1) to 16 h 
(R3) increased LAS removal from 34.8% to 51.8%. This performance 
gain is consistent with the hypothesis that the structural recalcitrance of 
the sulfonated aromatic group may require a longer kinetic window to 
accommodate the relatively slow metabolic adaptation of anaerobic 
consortia (Corada-Fern´andez et al., 2018). The limitation observed at 8 
h aligns with the findings of Carneiro et al. (2024), who reported that 
short residence times (e.g., 6 h) in anaerobic stages are often insufficient 
for the effective biotransformation of complex aromatic rings, resulting 
in negligible removal of recalcitrant micropollutants. In these systems, 
cleavage of the benzene ring under strictly reductive conditions is the 
rate-limiting step. The longer contact time in the 16-h configuration may 
have helped alleviate mass-transfer and reaction-rate constraints that 
commonly limit degradation in high-rate anaerobic systems.
The introduction of microaeration was associated with a further in­
crease in LAS removal, with the highest efficiency observed in R4 (64.0 
± 6.2%). While oxygen availability might have activated mono­
oxygenases and dioxygenases in both microaerated reactors, the longer 
contact time in R4 may have favored the progression of oxygen- 
dependent transformation steps proposed for LAS degradation. Ac­
cording to previously described LAS degradation pathways, oxygen- 
dependent reactions may decrease the molecule's hydrophobicity 
through oxidative transformations that generate more hydrophilic in­
termediates, including sulfophenylcarboxylates (SPCs) (Liu et al., 2024; 
Zhou et al., 2022). Although these intermediates were not directly 
quantified in the present study, the higher LAS removal observed in R4 is

occurred under microaerated conditions.

growing methanogens (Braga et al., 2015). While microaeration in R2

constrained the progression of LAS biotransformation. Conversely, the

longer contact time favored the progression of successive transformation

3.3. Microbial dynamics during the removal of LAS
3.3.1. Microbial community richness and diversity
The analysis of richness and diversity indices reveals a clear influ­
ence of microaeration on microbial community complexity and struc­
tural stability within the UASB systems (Table S1).
According to Chao1 and ACE indices, reactors operated under 
microaerated conditions exhibited higher microbial richness than their 
conventional counterparts, indicating that low oxygen availability pro­
moted the establishment of a broader range of taxa. Similarly, Shannon 
and Simpson indices indicated that microaerated systems supported 
higher diversity, reflecting a more even distribution of taxa and reduced 
dominance. This pattern suggests that microaeration may have 
increased redox heterogeneity, enabling the coexistence of facultative, 
strictly anaerobic, and oxygen-tolerant microorganisms, thereby 
increasing functional redundancy and metabolic versatility.
The inoculum exhibited intermediate richness and diversity, lower 
than those observed in the microaerated reactors but higher than in the 
conventional UASB systems. In contrast, its diversity indices were 
comparable to the microaerated condition, indicating a relatively 
balanced community. Upon reactor operation, conventional UASB 
conditions, particularly at short HRT, exerted strong selective pressure, 
reducing richness and favoring fast-growing fermentative taxa. In 
contrast, microaeration mitigated this effect by expanding redox niches 
and sustaining a broader range of functionally relevant microorganisms, 
including syntrophic bacteria and methanogens.
This structuring effect is further supported by the Venn diagram 
analysis, which demonstrates pronounced differentiation among com­
munities (Fig. S2). The inoculum contained a large number of unique 
ASVs, reflecting its heterogeneous origin. At the same time, all reactors 
developed distinct assemblages with comparable numbers of exclusive 
ASVs, indicating rapid community reorganization driven by operational 
conditions. The progressive increase in unique ASVs across the reactor 
configurations highlights the influence of the different operational 
conditions in expanding ecological niche space and enabling the estab­
lishment of specialized populations associated with LAS transformation 
and methanogenic activity.
The limited number of ASVs shared among all systems underscores 
the strong selective pressure imposed by reactor operation. It indicates 
that LAS degradation depended on reactor-specific microbial assemblies 
rather than on a conserved core microbiome. In microaerated reactors, a 
higher proportion of exclusive ASVs reflects greater functional diversi­
fication and community resilience, consistent with their superior per­
formance in LAS removal. Overall, these results demonstrate that

3.3.2. Microbial community structure
The microbial community structure differed among the hydraulic/ 
loading and microaeration conditions evaluated (Fig. 5).
At the phylum level, Proteobacteria dominated across all systems, 
which aligns with their central role in the anaerobic transformation of 
complex organic compounds, including surfactants, via fermentative 
and facultative pathways (de Barros et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020). 
Relative to the inoculum, a reduction in Caldisericota and Chloroflexi was 
observed, particularly under the 8-h HRT, indicating that short contact 
times imposed strong selective pressure against slow-growing syntro­
phic and filamentous taxa involved in biomass structuring and long- 
chain organic matter conversion.
A comparison between the conventional UASB reactors operated at 8 
h HRT (R1) and 16 h HRT (R3) highlights the role of residence time in 
shaping metabolic specialization and syntrophic stability. In R1, 
enrichment of Firmicutes alongside Proteobacteria may have favored fast 
fermentative metabolism, with dominance of Enterobacterales, Veillo­
nellales, and Selenomonadales, and families associated with acidogenesis 
and the rapid conversion of readily biodegradable substrates into short- 
chain fatty acids and alcohols (do Nascimento et al., 2021; Zígolo et al., 
2020).
The stimulation of Anaeromusa–Anaeroarcus, absent in the inoculum, 
further reflects selection for rapid fermentative pathways. Although 
such organisms may contribute to partial LAS transformation via co- 
metabolism and desulfonation, their metabolic orientation favors 
rapid carbon turnover rather than complete mineralization or stable 
syntrophic interactions with methanogens (Costa et al., 2024; Terreros- 
Mecalco et al., 2024). This configuration may help explain the lower LAS 
removal and moderate methane production in R1, along with inhibition 
of Methanosaetaceae, leading to sustained methane formation via less 
efficient fermentative and incomplete oxidation pathways.
In contrast, R3 exhibited a community structure indicative of 
enhanced process stability and syntrophic integration. The persistence 
of Caldisericota and enrichment of Anaerolineales reflect improved 
adaptation to slow hydrolysis, biomass structuring, and interspecies 
metabolite exchange. At the genus level, the co-occurrence of Caldiser­
icum, Methanosaeta, and Longilinea indicates a tighter integration among 
fermentative, acetogenic, and acetoclastic methanogenic pathways. The 
greater abundance of Methanosaetaceae at the longer HRT suggests that 
this operational condition may have favored the establishment of these 
populations, which is particularly relevant for LAS degradation, where 
acetate is produced gradually through complex transformation path­
ways. Despite lower methane production than in R1, the higher LAS 
removal in R3 indicates greater progression of LAS transformation under 
the longer contact time.

methanogenesis. A plausible explanation is the rapid consumption of the 
limited oxygen supply by facultative and oxygen-utilizing microorgan­

restricting oxygen penetration into the biomass. In addition, mass-

strictly anaerobic methanogens could remain active. Thus, the coexis­

microaeration is consistent with spatially heterogeneous oxygen avail­
ability within the sludge blanket. However, because spatial DO and ORP 
profiles were not measured, the establishment and distribution of these 
microenvironments cannot be directly confirmed from the present data.
Overall, comparisons within each HRT indicate that microaeration 
was associated with distinct microbial communities and greater LAS 
removal. Among the configurations evaluated, R4 achieved the highest 
LAS removal and exhibited a microbial profile with greater represen­

oxidative, and methanogenic functions.
3.3.3. Metabolic pathway analysis and functional implications
The distribution of metabolic pathways across the reactors reflected 
the selective pressures imposed by hydraulic retention time and 
microaeration and was fully consistent with the previously described 
microbial community structures (Fig. 6 and S3-S5).
In the conventional UASB operated at 8-h HRT, the dominance of 
sucrose metabolism, the TCA pathway, ω-oxidation, and sulfur meta­
bolism indicates a system primarily oriented toward rapid fermentative 
activity and incomplete oxidation processes.
This functional profile is consistent with the enrichment of Proteo­
bacteria and Firmicutes-related taxa, particularly Enterobacteriaceae, 
Sporomusaceae, and Anaeromusa–Anaeroarcus, which favor rapid sub­
strate turnover but provide limited metabolic continuity for the com­
plete degradation of complex molecules such as LAS (Carosia et al., 
2014). Functional prediction suggested the presence of ω-oxidation 
pathways potentially associated with Anaeromusa-Anaeroarcus and 
Rhodococcus, indicating a possible capacity for initial alkyl chain 
activation.
In the microaerated UASB operated at 8-h HRT, the metabolic profile 
shifted toward pathways associated with improved energy conservation, 
with dominance of the Acetyl-CoA pathway and both hydrogenotrophic 
and acetoclastic methanogenesis. This configuration reflects a more 
organized metabolic sequence in which fermentative and acetogenic 
reactions were efficiently aligned with methane formation. Meth­
anosaeta emerged as a central genus across all methanogenic routes, 
alongside Methanobacterium and Methanospirillum, which together 
facilitated efficient hydrogen consumption and acetate utilization.
Functional inference indicated that microaeration was associated 
with an increased genetic potential for ω-oxidation pathways involving 
Longilinea, Desulfovibrio, and Anaeromusa-Anaeroarcus, suggesting a 
possible enhancement in alkyl chain activation. Predicted β-oxidation 
pathways associated with Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter further indi­
cate potential for processing of fatty acid intermediates. In addition, the 
inferred participation of Thauera and Methanosaeta in aromatic com­
pound metabolism suggests a capacity to destabilize benzene rings. 
However, as these results are based on gene prediction rather than 
transcriptomic, proteomic, or metabolomic evidence, they represent 
potential metabolic capabilities that may help explain the higher LAS 
removal observed in R2 compared with the conventional reactor at the 
same HRT.

whether the proposed oxidative and anaerobic pathways occurred under 
the conditions evaluated.
3.4. Gas-phase oxygen depletion in microaerated reactors using nitrogen 
as an internal tracer
Off-gas monitoring provided additional evidence of the fate of the 
oxygen supplied to the microaerated reactors. Residual O2 remained low 
throughout operation, ranging from 0.20 to 1.22% in R2 and from 1.12 
to 2.16% in R4 (Fig. S6). More importantly, the O2/N2 ratio remained 
consistently below 0.25 in the synthetic air supplied to both reactors. 
This distinction is relevant because CH4 and CO2 production dilutes O2 
and N2 simultaneously and, in the absence of preferential O2 depletion, 
would not substantially alter their ratio. The consistently lower O2/N2 
values therefore indicate selective depletion of O2 during reactor pas­
sage rather than merely dilution of the inlet gas by biologically produced 
gases.
This behavior resulted in high apparent gas-phase O2 depletion 
throughout the experimental period, averaging 82.9 ± 5.7% in R2 and 
83.1 ± 3.3% in R4 (Fig. S7). The similar depletion observed at both 
HRTs indicates that the supplied oxygen was extensively depleted under 
both microaerated configurations despite their different hydraulic and 
organic loading conditions. Importantly, this high O2 depletion occurred 
without suppression of methanogenesis. R2 and R4 maintained methane 
production of approximately 2.6 and 1.4 L CH4 d⁻1, respectively, while 
their specific methane yields reached 0.24 ± 0.01 and 0.28 ± 0.01 L CH4 
gCODapp⁻1. The simultaneous occurrence of extensive O2 depletion and 
sustained methane formation supports the establishment of limited ox­
ygen availability rather than unrestricted aerobic conditions within the 
microaerated systems.

The characterization and control of very low oxygen availability in 
anaerobic systems remains analytically challenging. ORP-based control 
represents an important approach for this purpose because changes in 
redox potential can provide an indirect response to oxygen addition 
even when dissolved O2 concentrations are below the reliable detection 
range of conventional probes. Nguyen et al. (2019), for example, 
developed an intermittent microaeration strategy in which O2 injection 
was controlled by increasing the ORP by 25 mV relative to the corre­
sponding anaerobic baseline. This approach was subsequently applied to 
characterize microbial adaptation under microaerobic conditions (Wu 
et al., 2021) and, more recently, to control in-situ microaeration dur­
ing anaerobic co-digestion (Chuenchart et al., 2025). Importantly, ORP 
reflects the overall redox state of the medium and is influenced not only 
by O2 availability but also by electron acceptors and reducing equiva­
lents as well as operational conditions such as pH, conductivity, and 
temperature (Wu et al., 2021). Therefore, ORP monitoring would have 
provided valuable complementary information on the redox conditions 
established within the sludge bed, and its absence is recognized as a 
limitation of the present study.
Gas-phase monitoring has also been used as an operational indicator 
of microaeration in anaerobic digesters, with airflow adjusted according 
to residual O2 concentrations in the produced gas (Khadir et al., 2025). 
Here, rather than inferring a specific ORP or dissolved O2 condition, the 
controlled low air supply was complemented by direct chromatographic 
monitoring of O2 and N2 in the off-gas. The consistently low residual O2 
concentrations and marked decrease in the O2/N2 ratio relative to the 
synthetic-air reference provide independent evidence that most of the 
supplied O2 was depleted during reactor passage.
The gas-phase evidence is also consistent with the microbial struc­
ture observed in R2 and R4, where facultative and potentially oxygen- 
utilizing populations coexisted with methanogenic archaea, including 
Methanosaeta and members of Methanosarciniales. Rapid O2 utilization in 
oxygen-exposed regions of the sludge bed, combined with mass-transfer 
limitations within the granular biomass, may have preserved oxygen- 
depleted niches capable of sustaining methanogenesis. Similar coexis­
tence between facultative bacteria and methanogenic archaea has been 
reported under ORP-controlled microaeration, where limited O2 expo­
sure promoted functional adaptation without suppressing methane- 
producing populations (Nguyen et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021). Such 
spatial and functional coexistence provides a plausible ecological 
explanation for the increase in LAS removal observed under microaer­
ation, from 34.8 to 43.8% at 8 h and from 51.8 to 64.0% at 16 h, while 
anaerobic carbon conversion was maintained. Taken together, the 
controlled oxygen input, extensive gas-phase O2 depletion, sustained 
methanogenesis, and microbial community structure support the 
establishment of limited oxygen availability within the microaerated 
reactors. Nevertheless, because ORP and dissolved O2 were not directly 
monitored within the sludge bed, the spatial distribution and absolute 
redox conditions established inside the reactors cannot be resolved from 
the present dataset.
4. Conclusions
Microbial community analysis showed that the highest LAS removal 
(64%) in R4 was associated with a distinct microbial community char­
acterized by enrichment of facultative and microaerophilic genera, 
including Thauera and Desulfovibrio, along with acetoclastic metha­
nogens such as Methanosaeta. Functional predictions further indicated 
greater representation of oxygenase-related genes under microaeration, 
suggesting the potential for oxidative transformations to complement 
downstream anaerobic metabolism. These predictions, however, repre­
sent genetic potential rather than direct evidence of pathway expression 
or enzymatic activity.
Overall, microaeration combined with the longer HRT evaluated (16 
h) provided the best LAS removal among the tested configurations while 
maintaining methanogenesis, demonstrating the potential of controlled 
oxygen supplementation to intensify predominantly anaerobic treat­
ment of LAS-containing wastewater. From an implementation perspec­
tive, the results indicate that microaeration may be integrated into 
anaerobic treatment as a complementary strategy to enhance surfactant 
biotransformation without replacing the anaerobic process and its 
associated energy-recovery potential. Nevertheless, because HRT and 
OLR varied concomitantly between the 8-h and 16-h conditions, the 
superior performance of R4 should be interpreted as the response of the 
overall operational configuration rather than an isolated effect of HRT.
Although the combined reactor performance and microbial data 
support enhanced LAS biotransformation under microaeration, the lack 
of direct characterization of transformation products precludes defini­
tive reconstruction of the metabolic pathway. Future studies coupling 
targeted or untargeted mass spectrometry with microbial functional 
analyses are therefore needed to identify LAS intermediates and confirm 
the transformation pathways suggested by the present results.
